title: Three degrees (CCC 1554–1571)

cards: Sunday Mass in a parish church. A man in a white alb, a stole worn across one shoulder like a sash, reads the Gospel and later sets the table at the altar.

Another, the stole hanging straight down around his neck, says the Eucharistic prayer. And once in a while a third arrives with a tall pointed hat and a shepherd's staff, and it feels like an occasion.
Three men, three roles at one altar. A visitor might read three job titles on an org chart. The Church tells it as one sacrament.

teach.b: Back on day one hundred thirty-one, you met ordination. Today, its shape. The Catechism says Holy Orders is one sacrament in three degrees: bishops, priests and deacons.

The bishop's ordination, it says, is the fullness of the sacrament. Catholic teaching sees bishops as successors of the apostles. A bishop teaches, sanctifies and governs a local church, and he alone ordains others.
Priests, the Catechism says, are co-workers of the bishops.

teach.h: THE PRIEST: CO-WORKER WITH THE BISHOP.
teach.b: A priest doesn't minister on his own authority: he works in communion with his bishop, and at ordination promises him respect and obedience.
In the parish he celebrates the Eucharist, hears confessions and anoints the sick.
Then deacons, and here the Catechism makes a point worth hearing slowly: deacons are ordained not to the priesthood, but to service.

In Acts, the apostles ask the community to choose seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and wisdom, to look after the daily distribution of food, so the apostles can give themselves to prayer and the word.

Catholic tradition links the deacon's office to that story. A deacon baptizes, proclaims the Gospel, preaches, assists at the altar, witnesses marriages, leads funerals, and gives himself to works of charity.
The Latin Church, the Catechism notes, restored the deacon as a permanent ministry, one that can be given to married men.
Ignatius of Antioch, whom the Catechism quotes, holds the three together: respect the deacons, the bishop and the presbyters, he says, for without them there is no church.
One sacrament, held three ways, for serving one people.

how: In the Catholic Church a bishop ordains bishops, priests and deacons by laying hands on them and saying the prayer of consecration; the three serve together in the diocese and the parish.

games.q: you're one of the apostles. the community is growing, the daily food distribution is going badly, and you have prayer and preaching to do. what do you do?
o: stop preaching and run the kitchen yourselves.
ask the community to choose good men to serve.
let the problem sort itself out.
games.why: in Acts 6 the community chooses seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom, and the apostles pray and lay hands on them.

practice: If you know a deacon, picture him: maybe a man who works a weekday job, preaches on Sunday and visits the hospital on Tuesday night.
If you don't, picture someone who serves your community without being noticed, who stacks chairs, drives people to appointments, sits with the grieving.
If you pray, ask God to sustain that service; if you don't, hold them in gratitude for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Three degrees. One sacrament of Holy Orders, given to bishops, priests and deacons: the fullness, the co-workers, and those ordained to service. Today's word.
